import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Prime quadruplet conjecture

*Reference:* [Prime quadruplet Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/prime_quadruplet)
-/

namespace PrimeQuadruplet

/--
Are there infinitely many prime quadruplets, where a prime quadruplet is a set of four primes
of the form $\{p, p + 2, p + 6, p + 8\}$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem prime_quadruplet :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ Prime (p + 2) ∧ Prime (p + 6) ∧ Prime (p + 8)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end PrimeQuadruplet
modeling_decisions: Interpreted a prime quadruplet, following the cited background article, as four primes of the form {p, p + 2, p + 6, p + 8}, and represented infinitely many such quadruplets by infinitude of the set of their natural-number starting values p.
Preserved the source's yes/no question using `answer(sorry) ↔ ...`; thus a positive answer is exactly the infinitude proposition.
Excluded the article's asymptotic formula, Brun's constant, and prime quintuplet/sextuplet questions because they are not part of the list-entry statement.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Prime quadruplets

A prime quadruplet is a set of four primes of the form $\{p, p + 2, p + 6, p + 8\}$.
This is the only prime constellation of length 4. The first prime quadruplets are
$\{5, 7, 11, 13\}$, $\{11, 13, 17, 19\}$ and $\{101, 103, 107, 109\}$.
It is not known whether there are infinitely many prime quadruplets; the conjectured
answer is yes.

*References:*
- [Prime quadruplet Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/prime_quadruplet)
- [List of unsolved problems in mathematics Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
-/

namespace PrimeQuadruplet

/--
Are there infinitely many prime quadruplets, i.e. infinitely many primes $p$ such that
$p + 2$, $p + 6$ and $p + 8$ are all prime?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem prime_quadruplet :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ Prime (p + 2) ∧ Prime (p + 6) ∧ Prime (p + 8)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end PrimeQuadruplet
modeling_decisions: Prime quadruplet is taken, per the Wikipedia article's definition, to be a set of four primes of the form {p, p+2, p+6, p+8}; the exceptional quadruplet {5, 7, 11, 13} is included (as the article does), and no 30n+11 restriction is imposed since it is a consequence, not part of the definition.
The question is a yes/no question, so it is formalized as `answer(sorry) ↔ S.Infinite`; `answer(True)` encodes the conjectured positive answer.

`Prime p` with `p : ℕ` is the root `Prime` (equivalent to `Nat.Prime` via `Nat.prime_iff`), following the idiom of the existing `TwinPrimes.lean` and `PrimeTriplets.lean`; scratch-checked that 5 and 11 lie in the set and 0 and 7 do not.

The article's Hardy–Littlewood asymptotic formula, Brun's constant B₄, and the quintuplet/sextuplet questions are not part of the posed list-entry question and are omitted, as prescribed by the decomposition table.

prime_quadruplet.why: Stated as `answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ Prime (p + 2) ∧ Prime (p + 6) ∧ Prime (p + 8)}.Infinite`, mirroring the TwinPrimes/PrimeTriplets idiom. A prime quadruplet {p, p+2, p+6, p+8} is determined by its least element p, so the set of such p being infinite is exactly 'infinitely many prime quadruplets'. Only existing Mathlib primitives (`Prime` on ℕ, `Set.Infinite`) are used.
